title: Need to unify handling of blocking JavaScript dialogs

labels.name: interop
labels.description: Implementations are not interoperable with each other

body:
Blocking JavaScript dialogs (`window.alert()`, `window.confirm()`, `window.prompt()`) were introduced with the first version of JavaScript in Netscape Navigator 2 in 1995. They are synchronous and blocking and are a relic of their time.

`window.confirm()` and `window.prompt()` are specifically problematic because they synchronously return a value; however, it is commonly assumed that `window.alert()` will pause execution while the dialog is up, so it deserves to be in this discussion.

In a multi-process UA, implementing these dialogs is difficult. Because these functions return a value, the JS engine must pause while the dialog is displayed. There may be more than one page that shares the render process (and perhaps is even required to share the JS engine) with a page showing a dialog, so if a page is showing a dialog, there's no telling which other pages that the UA is showing are blocked and unable to process user interaction. This is a tricky constraint for UAs.

The naïve approach is to use an app-modal dialog for showing these dialogs, and to activate the tab showing them. This solves the shared-process problem: if a page shows a dialog, it jumps to the front and blocks the user from switching away from it. In this way, there's no way a user can find themselves interacting with a page that is frozen because a sibling tab is blocked on a dialog.

This is obviously unacceptable, as it is abusable (and is abused) by bad actors. Different browsers have solved this problem in different ways, but this is not good for the web platform. We should agree on a solution.

**Safari**

Safari (as of 9.1) does not activate tabs showing dialogs. If a tab in the background attempts to show a dialog, no activation happens. However, if the tab in the foreground shares the same JS engine/render process with the tab showing the dialog, the pausing of the JS engine for the background tab showing the dialog also pauses the tab in the foreground. (This bug was [reported to Apple](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=155925).)

**Firefox**

Firefox does not activate tabs by default when they show dialogs. If a tab in the background attempts to show a dialog, other pages continue running. This is achieved by running nested event loops, which causes issues when multiple pages close dialogs in a different order than they were opened, issues when pages can script other pages that should be blocked, etc.

**Chrome**

Chrome does not activate tabs showing dialogs. Because there is no guarantee that the page that the user is interacting with doesn't share a render process with any page showing a dialog, Chrome will simply not block for `window.confirm()` and `window.prompt()` but will return `false` if the page calling those functions isn't the active tab of the frontmost window. `window.alert()` is a little more involved. If `window.alert()` is called by the active tab of the frontmost window, the page will pause while the dialog is up, but if the user switches away from the current tab, or if `window.alert()` is called by a tab that isn't the active tab of the frontmost window, `window.alert()` will return immediately before blocking (although Chrome will display the dialog without blocking the page when the page comes to the front again). (The [design doc](http://bit.ly/project-oldspice) has more explanation.)

**Edge**

Edge does not activate tabs showing dialogs. I have been unable to divine its implementation from experimentation. If anyone can clarify how it works, that would be appreciated.

At least three of the four major browsers solve this problem in different ways, and the fourth might as well. Chrome chose its approach specifically after seeing and choosing to not take the approaches of Safari and Firefox, and so that's the approach we recommend the standard take. However, it's time to take action here. We need to decide on an approach that is 1) implementable, 2) user acceptable, and 3) not horrifically breaking of the web, and standardize it.
